title: Mock paper 1
intro:
**120 minutes · 100 marks.** Same structure as the final paper:

| Section | Marks | What |
|---|---|---|
| A - MCQ | 50 | 3 scenarios × 5 questions, then 10 theory questions (2 marks each) |
| B - Code-based | 40 | 8 questions × 5: fill the gaps, arrange the lines, spot the bug |
| C - Full code | 10 | One complete program, self-marked against a rubric |

Fill-the-gap and arrange questions earn partial credit; MCQs and spot-the-line are all or nothing. You can flag questions and come back. Answers save in this browser as you go.

sections.title: Section A - MCQ
sections.blurb: Each scenario describes a program and what was observed when it ran; five questions follow it. Questions 16–25 are on the theory. 2 marks each, one answer is correct.

scenarios.title: Scenario 1 · Ticket counter
Scenario 2 · Print spooler
Scenario 3 · Photo filter in OpenMP

questions.prompt: Why does version A print a different value below 400 000 on every run?
options: At `-O0` the compiler drops some loop iterations
`long` is too small to hold 400 000 on a 64-bit machine
`printf` inside the threads delays some sellers so they finish after `main` prints
`sold++` is a load, an add and a store; two threads can load the same value and both store value + 1, so one increment is lost
questions.explain: A read-modify-write on shared memory is not atomic. Overlapping load–store windows lose updates; how many depends on the interleaving, so the total changes from run to run.

questions.prompt: Versions B and C are both correct. Why is C about 100 times faster than B?
options: C makes 4 lock/unlock calls in total, B makes 400 000 on one contended mutex, serialising the loop and bouncing the lock between cores
C uses more threads than B
The mutex in B is a spin lock, which is always slower than a sleep lock
B is compiled without optimisation and C with optimisation
questions.explain: Shrink the critical section and lock rarely: private accumulation followed by one combine. OpenMP `reduction` and split counters are the same idea.

questions.prompt: Why do the start-up lines sometimes show the same seller id twice and never id 0?
options: `pthread_create` does not start threads in creation order
Every thread receives the address of the single loop variable `i`, which has usually changed (or reached 4) by the time a thread reads it
Thread ids are reused once a thread has finished
`printf` is not thread-safe, so lines get mixed up
questions.explain: Pass the value, not the address: `(void *)(intptr_t)i`, or a separate array slot per thread.

questions.prompt: In version B a developer deletes the `pthread_mutex_unlock(&m)` line. What happens?
options: The total is still correct but the program is slower
The program crashes with a segmentation fault
The first thread increments once, then blocks re-locking the mutex it already holds; every other thread blocks too and the program hangs
The program runs normally because the mutex is released when the loop iteration ends
questions.explain: A default mutex is not recursive: re-locking it from the owning thread blocks forever. All other threads wait on the same lock - the process sits at 0 % CPU.

questions.prompt: Version A is rebuilt with `-O2` and now prints 400 000 every time. What is the right conclusion?
options: The program is now correct and needs no lock
The race is still there; the optimiser turned the loop into a single `sold += 100000`, so the race window became tiny
With optimisation the threads run one after another
questions.explain: Passing a test is not proof of correctness. With `-O0` or `volatile` the lost updates return.

questions.prompt: What is the most likely cause of a printer "printing a garbage job"?
options: The waits use `if`, so a printer that wakes up (spuriously, or after another printer took the job) does not re-check `count == 0` and reads an empty slot
The queue capacity of 8 is too small
`pthread_cond_signal` was called while holding the mutex
The modulo arithmetic on `head` is wrong
questions.explain: Pthreads condition variables are Mesa-style and allow spurious wake-ups. Always wait in a `while` loop that re-tests the predicate.

questions.prompt: The freeze with a full queue and everyone blocked is best explained by:
options: The `STOP` jobs arrived before the normal jobs
With one condition variable, a printer's `signal` woke another printer or a workstation instead of a waiting one that could proceed, so the useful waiter slept on (a lost wake-up)
A deadlock caused by two mutexes taken in different orders
questions.explain: Use two condition variables (`not_full`, `not_empty`) so a signal always reaches a thread that can act on it - or use `broadcast` with `while` loops.

questions.prompt: The spooler is reconfigured with **4 printers** but still 3 workstations, each sending one `STOP`. What happens at shutdown?
options: Three printers exit; the fourth blocks for ever in `take()` on an empty queue, so `main` never returns from joining it
The workstations block because the queue is full of `STOP` jobs
One printer prints a `STOP` job as if it were a document
questions.explain: Every consumer needs its own termination signal: send one `STOP` per printer (or have each printer count `STOP`s from every producer).

questions.prompt: Which ordering guarantee does the spooler give?
options: Jobs leave the queue in the order they were inserted, but with two printers two jobs from one workstation can finish printing in either order
Jobs from different workstations are never interleaved
Jobs always finish printing in the order they were submitted
There is no ordering at all, even for removal from the queue
questions.explain: A FIFO queue orders removal, not completion. Once two consumers work in parallel, finishing order depends on scheduling.

questions.prompt: The queue capacity is changed from 8 to 1. Which statement is true?
options: Jobs are taken out of order
Printers can now take the same job twice
It is still correct, but producers and consumers now alternate in lock-step, causing many more waits and context switches and lower throughput
questions.explain: Correctness does not depend on the capacity; a larger buffer only absorbs bursts so the two sides block less often.

questions.prompt: What is the best fix for loop 2, and why?
options: `#pragma omp critical` around `bright++`, because it is the most general
`reduction(+:bright)`: each thread counts privately and the copies are combined once at the end
questions.explain: `private` would throw the per-thread counts away; critical and atomic are correct but pay a synchronisation per hit (0.31 s and 0.12 s vs 0.015 s).

questions.prompt: Why is `atomic` (0.12 s) faster than `critical` (0.31 s) but still much slower than `reduction`?
options: Atomic runs the loop on fewer threads
Atomic is a single hardware read-modify-write instead of a lock acquire/release, but every hit still contends for the same cache line; reduction has no shared writes inside the loop
questions.explain: Cost order: critical (lock per hit) > atomic (contended atomic instruction per hit) > reduction (private work, one combine).

questions.prompt: Why does loop 3 barely speed up, and what should change?
options: Rows must be processed in order, so the loop cannot be parallelised
Static scheduling gives each thread a contiguous block of rows; the threads owning the expensive middle rows finish last while the others idle. Use `schedule(dynamic)` (or `guided`)
The loop has a data race; add `reduction`
Four threads are too few; use 64 threads
questions.explain: Load imbalance. Dynamic scheduling hands out rows (or small chunks) to whichever thread is free, at the cost of a shared counter per chunk.

questions.prompt: Loop 1 is switched from the default schedule to `schedule(dynamic, 1)`. What is the most likely effect?
options: Wrong output, because rows are processed out of order
No gain, possibly slightly slower: the rows already cost the same, so static was balanced and dynamic only adds scheduling overhead
The program deadlocks at the implicit barrier
About 4 times faster, because dynamic is always better
questions.explain: Dynamic scheduling pays off only when iteration costs vary.

questions.prompt: What do the debug lines print?
options: An indeterminate value in each thread - a `private` copy is uninitialised; `firstprivate(level)` would print 5
The thread number in each thread
questions.explain: `private` creates a new uninitialised variable per thread (GCC warns about it). After the region, the original `level` is still 5.

questions.prompt: 90 % of a program can be parallelised perfectly. What is the best possible speedup on 8 cores, and on unlimited cores?
Two processes each execute 3 atomic actions. How many different interleavings are possible?
A computation has work $T_1 = 1000$ and span $T_\infty = 50$. What is the best lower bound on $T_{40}$?
questions.explain: Work law $T_P \ge T_1/P = 25$, span law $T_P \ge T_\infty = 50$; the bound is the larger, 50. Parallelism $T_1/T_\infty = 20$ - more than 20 processors cannot help.

questions.prompt: In Peterson's algorithm, both processes set their flag and then write `victim`. Which process enters if both arrive together?
options: The one that did NOT write `victim` last
The one with the lower id
questions.explain: Each writes `victim = me` ("you go first"). Whoever writes last sees its own id and waits; the other proceeds.

questions.prompt: Two processes each "test the other's flag, then set my own flag" before entering. Which property fails?
options: Mutual exclusion - both can test before either sets, and both enter
Deadlock freedom - both wait for ever
Livelock freedom - both keep backing off
questions.explain: The test and the set are separate steps; the interleaving test, test, set, set lets both in.

questions.prompt: Making every thread acquire locks in one global order prevents deadlock by removing which condition?
questions.explain: With a global order, a chain of waiting threads can never close into a cycle.

questions.prompt: A semaphore initialised to 1 protects a critical section. Which invariant proves mutual exclusion?
options: $S \le 0$ whenever a process is in the CS and $S = 2$ otherwise
questions.explain: From $S = S_0 + \#\text{post} - \#\text{wait}$ and $\#CS = \#\text{wait} - \#\text{post}$: $S + \#CS = 1$, and $S \ge 0$ gives $\#CS \le 1$.

questions.prompt: Pthreads and Java monitors use signal-and-continue (Mesa) semantics. What must a waiting thread do as a result?
options: Release the monitor lock before calling `wait`
Re-check its condition in a `while` loop after waking
Nothing - the condition is guaranteed true on wake-up
questions.explain: The signaller keeps running; another thread may change the state before the waiter re-acquires the lock.

questions.prompt: Under Flynn's taxonomy, a GPU running one kernel over thousands of data elements is best described as:
options: SIMD (NVIDIA calls it SIMT: warps of threads execute one instruction together)
questions.explain: One instruction stream applied to many data elements, in lock-step within a warp.

questions.prompt: An increment written as a compare-and-swap retry loop is:
questions.explain: A CAS fails only because another thread's CAS succeeded - the system progresses - but one unlucky thread can retry without bound.

sections.title: Section B - Code-based
sections.blurb: 8 questions, 5 marks each. Choose the missing lines, drag the lines into order (or use the arrows), or click the faulty line(s).

questions.prompt: Complete `put()` of a bounded buffer protected by one mutex and two condition variables.
questions.explain: Wait in a `while` on `not_full`; advance `tail` circularly; then signal `not_empty`, the condition the consumer waits on.

questions.prompt: Arrange `get()` of the bounded buffer in a correct order.
questions.explain: Lock, wait while empty, take the item, update head and count, wake a producer, unlock, return. Returning before unlocking would leave the mutex locked forever.

questions.prompt: This thread function is meant to count in a local variable and add to the shared `counter` once, under the lock. Click the line(s) that make it pointlessly slow.
questions.explain: `local` is private to the thread - locking around `local++` (lines 4 and 6) protects nothing and brings back the contention of locking every single increment. Only the final `counter += local` needs the lock.

questions.prompt: Complete this OpenMP Monte Carlo estimate of π with a reduction and a private random seed.
questions.explain: `reduction(+:count)` gives each thread a private zeroed `count` and sums them at the end. The seed must differ per thread and live inside the region; `rand_r` takes a pointer to it.

questions.prompt: The two-phase reusable barrier below has one wrong line. Click it.
questions.explain: The last thread out of phase 1 must close turnstile 1 and **open turnstile 2**: `sem_wait(&b->t1); sem_post(&b->t2);`. Line 8 posts t1 again, so t2 never opens and every thread blocks on line 10.

questions.prompt: Arrange a lock-free compare-and-swap increment loop in order.
questions.explain: Read the current value, try to swap in old+1; if another thread changed `counter` in between, the CAS fails and the loop re-reads. Lock-free, not wait-free.

questions.prompt: Complete the hand-over-hand `fine_contains` (sentinel head node with key `INT_MIN`).
questions.explain: Lock the next node **before** releasing the previous one - that is the hand-over-hand rule. Releasing `pred` first opens a gap where `curr` can be deleted under you.

questions.prompt: Arrange a thread-pool worker that grabs the next task index under a mutex.
questions.explain: Take and increment the shared index inside the critical section, release it **before** doing the (long) task, and stop when the index runs past the end. Doing the task while holding the lock would serialise the pool.

sections.title: Section C - Full code
sections.blurb: One complete program, 10 marks. After you submit, the model solution and a marking rubric appear - tick what you achieved.

questions.prompt:
Write a complete C program (pthreads) with **one producer and one consumer** sharing a **circular bounded buffer of size 5**.

- The producer puts the integers `0 … N−1` (N from `argv[1]`), then a sentinel `-1`.
- The consumer prints every item and stops at the sentinel.
- Use **one mutex and two condition variables**; neither thread may busy-wait.
- `main` creates both threads, joins them and prints `All items consumed.`

rubric.text: Shared state: circular buffer, head, tail, count, one mutex, two condition variables, correctly initialised
`put` waits in a **while** loop on `not_full` while the buffer is full
`get` waits in a **while** loop on `not_empty` while the buffer is empty
Indices advance modulo the buffer size and `count` is updated inside the lock
Each side signals the *other* condition (`put` → not_empty, `get` → not_full) and unlocks on every path
Producer sends the sentinel; consumer stops on it and does not print it
`main` parses N, creates and joins both threads, prints the final line

questions.explain: Compare your code with the model solution line by line, then tick each rubric item you fully satisfied. Common slips: `if` instead of `while`, signalling the same CV you wait on, or returning from `get` before unlocking.
